doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Jazz records, vaudeville and starting out
title: Disdain for careless lyrics and the value of a strict schooling
summary: She complains that modern lyrics do not even rhyme and says her schooling taught her to keep working until she got things right.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Years have passed, and at the time I thought it wasn’t all that great, but now when I hear the average lyric that somebody writes, that they’re so puerile, and they don’t even . . . nothing rhymes. People don’t bother to rhyme, like “house” with “mouse.” They put “house” and some other word which maybe sounded the same. People don’t take any trouble any more.
That’s a breakdown in the ability of mastering the language, which is likewise another conversation to go through as well. [laughs]

Yes, right, but it seems to have to do with nobody having the . . . taking trouble, whatever that instinct is, to work at it ’til you get it right. That’s one of the things I was glad of getting a good schooling, because they just . . . you just worked at it until you got it right. There was no margin for error. You couldn’t say, “I can’t do that.” It was like, “Well, you’ve got to do it.” And so we did.
Which is a good thing. Years later, I realized it was a good thing.
